title: Sound
ks3: Waves: sound, vibrations, loudness and pitch, hearing and the speed of sound
intro: Sound is made by vibrations. Practise how sound travels, loudness and pitch, how we hear, echoes and the speed of sound.
description: Free KS3 Physics sound questions with answers: vibrations, how sound travels, amplitude and loudness, frequency and pitch, hearing range, echoes and the speed of sound. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: What makes a sound?
questions.hint: Touch your throat while you hum.
questions.explain: All sounds are made by something vibrating (moving backwards and forwards quickly), like a guitar string or your vocal cords.

questions.q: Sound cannot travel through…
questions.hint: Sound needs particles to pass the vibrations along.
questions.explain: Sound is passed on by particles bumping into each other. A vacuum has no particles, so sound can't travel through it. That is why space is silent.

questions.q: Sound usually travels fastest through…
questions.hint: In which state are the particles closest together?
questions.explain: The particles in solids are close together and strongly joined, so they pass vibrations on quickly. Sound travels about 15 times faster in steel than in air.

questions.q: Whales can hear each other's songs from far away under the sea. What does the sound travel through?
questions.hint: What is all around a whale?
questions.explain: The sound travels through the water. The water particles pass the vibrations along. Sound travels faster in water than in air.

questions.q: As a sound wave passes through the air, how do the air particles move?
options: They vibrate backwards and forwards, in the same direction the sound travels
They move up and down, across the direction the sound travels
They travel all the way from the sound to your ear
questions.hint: Think of a slinky spring being pushed and pulled from one end.
questions.explain: The particles vibrate backwards and forwards along the direction the sound travels, making squashed-up and spread-out regions. This kind of wave is called a longitudinal wave. The particles do not travel to your ear: only the vibration does.

questions.q: Two astronauts on the Moon, where there is no air, touch their helmets together. One shouts and the other hears a faint sound. How?
options: The vibrations pass through the solid helmets
The sound travels through the vacuum
The Moon has a little air that carries it
questions.hint: Sound can't travel through a vacuum, but it can travel through solids.
questions.explain: There is no air on the Moon, so sound can't travel across the gap. When the helmets touch, the vibrations pass through the solid helmets from one astronaut to the other.

questions.q: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.hint: It is named after the scientist Heinrich Hertz.
questions.explain: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). 1 Hz means one vibration each second.

questions.q: The number of vibrations each second is called the…
questions.hint: It is measured in hertz.
questions.explain: Frequency is how many vibrations (waves) there are each second.

questions.q: The two sound waves are drawn on the same scale. Which sound is louder?
questions.hint: Loudness depends on how tall the waves are (the amplitude).
questions.explain: Wave A has a bigger amplitude (taller waves), so A is louder. Both have the same number of waves, so the same pitch.

questions.q: The two sound waves are drawn on the same scale. Which sound has the higher pitch?
questions.hint: Pitch depends on how many waves fit in the same time (the frequency).
questions.explain: B has more waves in the same time, so it has a higher frequency and a higher pitch. Their heights are the same, so they are equally loud.

questions.q: You hit a drum harder. What happens to the sound?
questions.hint: Hitting harder makes the drum skin vibrate more.
questions.explain: A harder hit makes bigger vibrations (a bigger amplitude), so the sound is louder.

questions.q: The two sound waves are drawn on the same scale. Which sound is quieter and lower in pitch?
questions.hint: Quieter means smaller waves. Lower pitch means fewer waves in the same time.
questions.explain: A has smaller waves (a smaller amplitude), so it is quieter. A also has fewer waves in the same time (a lower frequency), so it has a lower pitch.

questions.q: A guitarist presses a string down so that a shorter part of it vibrates. The note gets higher. Why?
options: The shorter string vibrates more times each second
The shorter string vibrates with a bigger amplitude
The string vibrates fewer times each second
questions.hint: Pitch depends on the frequency.
questions.explain: A shorter string vibrates faster, so it has a higher frequency (more vibrations each second). A higher frequency means a higher pitch.

questions.q: Which part of the ear starts to vibrate first when sound arrives?
questions.hint: It is a thin skin stretched across the end of the ear canal.
questions.explain: Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate. The small bones pass the vibrations to the cochlea, which sends signals to the brain.

questions.q: Young people can usually hear sounds with frequencies from about…
questions.hint: The top of the range is about twenty thousand.
questions.explain: The human hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. The top of the range goes down as people get older.

questions.q: A dog whistle makes a sound of 30,000 Hz. Why can't people hear it?
options: It is above our hearing range (ultrasound)
It is below our hearing range
questions.hint: Compare 30,000 Hz with the top of the human hearing range.
questions.explain: 30,000 Hz is above 20,000 Hz, so it is ultrasound. Dogs can hear much higher frequencies than people.

questions.q: The loudness of a sound is measured in…
questions.hint: It is not hertz: that is for frequency.
questions.explain: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). A whisper is about 30 dB and a very loud concert can be over 100 dB.

questions.q: Why do people wear ear defenders at very loud places, like near a drill or at a loud concert?
options: Very loud sounds can damage the ear for good
Loud sounds make the eardrum stop vibrating
They make sounds higher in pitch
questions.hint: What can happen to your hearing after a lot of very loud noise?
questions.explain: Very loud sounds can damage the tiny hair cells in the cochlea. This damage can be permanent, so it is important to protect your ears.

questions.q: A microphone has a thin sheet inside (a diaphragm) that vibrates when sound hits it, a bit like your eardrum. What does a microphone do?
options: Changes sound into an electrical signal
Changes an electrical signal into sound
questions.hint: A microphone is plugged into a computer or amplifier. What goes along the wire?
questions.explain: The vibrating diaphragm makes an electrical signal that matches the sound. A loudspeaker does the opposite: it changes an electrical signal back into sound.

questions.q: Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air. How far does it travel in 3 s?
questions.hint: Distance = speed × time.

questions.q: You see lightning and hear the thunder 5 s later. Sound travels at about 340 m/s. About how far away is the storm?
questions.hint: The light reaches you almost straight away. The sound takes 5 s.
questions.explain: Distance = 340 m/s × 5 s = 1700 m (about 1.7 km).

questions.q: Someone shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
questions.hint: The sound goes to the cliff and back again.
questions.explain: In 2 s the sound travels 340 × 2 = 680 m. That is there and back, so the cliff is 680 ÷ 2 = 340 m away.

questions.q: Why do we see lightning before we hear the thunder?
options: Light travels much faster than sound
Our eyes work faster than our ears
questions.hint: Compare the speed of light with the speed of sound.
questions.explain: Light travels at about 300,000,000 m/s and sound at only about 340 m/s, so the light arrives almost at once and the sound later.

questions.q: What is an echo?
options: A sound that has reflected (bounced) off a surface
A sound that is very high-pitched
A sound that gets louder as it travels
questions.hint: Think of shouting in a big empty hall or towards a cliff.
questions.explain: An echo is a reflected sound. It bounces off a hard surface, like a wall or a cliff, and comes back to you a moment later.

questions.q: Sound travels at about 1500 m/s in sea water. A whale's call takes 4 s to reach a ship. How far away is the whale?
questions.hint: Distance = speed × time.
questions.explain: Distance = 1500 m/s × 4 s = 6000 m (6 km). Sound travels more than 4 times faster in water than in air.

questions.q: A ship sends a sound pulse down to the sea bed. The echo comes back 0.4 s later. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. How deep is the sea?
questions.hint: The sound goes down to the sea bed and back up again.
questions.explain: In 0.4 s the sound travels 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m. That is down and back, so the sea is 600 ÷ 2 = 300 m deep. Ships use this to measure depth (sonar).
